region.en: Crowded winter-house by the frozen sea

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Passed family to family until 'cast him out on the dunghill at once,' Iliarsorkik is taken in by a widow whose single lamp burns when all the others are dark. Sandpipers one a day, then partridges, then seals from the breathing-hole the mist revealed — he feeds the starving house, shares his seals with another starving widow on the way home, and kills an ice-covered bear by hollowing a cave in an iceberg and spearing it with his ice-pick at every pass. On the flensing road they find the corpses of those who died trying to reach the bear.
summary.zh: 被輾轉寄養、終被喝令『扔到糞堆上去』的孤兒伊利亞索基克，被一位寡婦收留——全屋燈熄之際，唯她的燈還亮著。磯鷸日增一只，繼而雷鳥，再繼而自霧中尋得的海豹呼吸孔——他餵活了一屋饑民，歸途又分海豹救了另一家瀕死之人；以鑿冰器環冰山鑿穴藏身，逐圈刺擊冰封巨熊，直至其倒斃。剝皮路上，他們見到那些試圖走到熊跟前而餓斃路旁的屍體。

sensitivity.note: Famine deaths recorded as told in the 1875 source. Widow-provider pattern recurs across the collection.

passages.text: In a house which was occupied by a great number of people lived a married couple with only one son; the parents, however, both died while he was quite a baby. Another family adopted him; but on finding that he gave them more trouble than they had expected, they soon grew tired of him, and he became nothing but a bore to them; others took him up, but in a little time neglected him; and thus it befell that all the families in a house came to take charge of him by turns. His last foster-parents had him for rather a long time; but on a certain day when the man happened to return home without any catch, and was cross and moody, he addressed his wife, saying, 'This boy is a mere good-for-nothing; cast him out on the dunghill at once.' Meantime a widow, whose son had just commenced to try his hand at seal-hunting, took him in; she brought him up, and he did well, and was well provided for from that time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One autumn the weather turned bad with heavy gales, and snowdrifts coming on earlier than usual, there had hardly been a chance of any catch for the inhabitants. Before the days had begun to lengthen the sea was quite frozen over, and the bad weather still continuing, the many hunters and providers about the place entirely ceased to go out; all their provisions had been spent, and the lamps were not lighted in the evening. The only lamp still burning was that of the widow, and the only person that made any attempt at hunting was her adopted son Iliarsorkik. One of his housemates, a man who did not possess any kayak, used to take him by the hand every morning and give him a run uphill; by continuing this exercise he soon got to be very swift and agile. Meanwhile the inmates of the crowded house all remained in bed for hunger and cold; but every evening the widow went to her little store and took out a handful of angmagsat (dried capelins, the chief winter provision), bestowing a small share upon each — her own son got four, her adopted son three, and the others half a one, all with a little morsel of blubber besides.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One morning at low tide Iliarsorkik saw some small spots off the rocky shore free of ice, and coming nearer saw a great number of little sandpipers there; he at length caught one and brought it to the house. 'Look here, what I have got!' — the men who lay on the ledge cried out, 'Oh, he has actually got a sandpiper!' and reproached each other for having driven him out, saying he might now have been able to provide for them. The mother cut the little bird through at all its joints, giving every one their share, but still some one went on crying for more. The next day Iliarsorkik brought two, and every succeeding day one more; the widow always divided them and gave their house-fellows something, each in turn. One day he again met the man who used to give him a turn up the hills, who pointed out to him a spot where the partridges were sitting in the snow with their black beaks peeping forth, directing him how to get at them; he brought one home the first day, every following day the number increased, and the men were constantly repeating, 'What a pity we ever cast him off from us!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day when he was away among the mountains in search of partridges with his friend, he observed a mist hanging above the waters, at one time growing thicker, and shortly after dissolving — his companions hailed it as a good sign, a sure token of holes in the ice kept open by the sea animals gathered there to breathe. They climbed a still higher mountain to make sure of the place; in the evening Iliarsorkik said to his brother, 'To-morrow I don't intend to hunt on shore; I shall just take a walk on the ice, and give a look round to find out the breathing-holes' — his foster-brother answered, 'Yonder beneath the boat thou wilt find my hunting-tools... but mind they are put deep down in the snow.' Early in the morning he was off, fell in with the frost-haze, followed its direction, and soon arrived at the brim of the aperture, where he saw the seals diving up and down and playing about in large crowds in the open water. Finding it difficult to get a sure footing on the slippery edge, he lost no time, took aim at once, and fixed his harpoon into one of the smaller seals; hauling it up on the ice, fastening it to his towing-line, he made the best of his way home. When the starving creatures heard him dragging a seal along through the house-passage a great clamour and strife ensued; the widow first cut very thin slices of blubber and skin together and handed them round — 'Each of you will get a piece in his or her turn' — took a piece of flesh of the size of a hand and boiled it after having lit some lamps; but even this meal did not satisfy them, and in the night some of them came creeping across the floor to steal the raw flesh, so faint they could not get back and climb the ledge. Iliarsorkik brought a larger seal on the following day, the widow now able to light all the lamps and warm up the house, though still very careful in sharing out very small rations; from this day forth Iliarsorkik every day brought home seals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One time when he had got two very big ones and was already half-way home, he was suddenly caught in an easterly gale with a snowstorm blowing right in his face, so that he was not able to see anything at all; continuing to walk straight against the wind, as it hauled round to the south he took a wrong direction and lost his way. Towards evening he concluded he must have gained the coast-side by the loose blocks of ice scattered about; leaving his seals on the beach, he stepped up on shore and came across a house. On entering it he saw only the foremost lamps burning, behind this a widow and a young man sitting, the latter with his chin buried deep in the fur collar of his jacket, but behind, in the more remote corner of the house, the lamps all extinguished. 'I have not absolutely come here on a visit, but I was not aware that the wind had changed, and thus lost my way in the snow-drift.' 'Then thou hadst better stay here till to-morrow; and when the weather alters for the better thou mayst return to thy home.' 'If ye have any fancy at all, ye are very welcome to one of my seals' — no sooner had he uttered these words than a faint sound of wailing was heard from the dark corners of the room: these people were likewise starving, and he had just come in time to save them. The weather being fine on the following day he reached his home, and when he had told his mother how he had solaced the hungry and starving, she answered him, 'Always act in that way, and the number of thy captured animals will always increase.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Another time when he was just making ready what he had caught to carry it home, he suddenly heard a tremendous roar, and the ice seemed to quake beneath his feet; looking round and seeing nothing but icebergs right and left, he thought it might have been one of them calving. When the roaring sound was again heard, and had come much nearer, he again turned round and saw that what he had taken for an iceberg was a great bear, all covered with ice, standing erect before him. When he saw the beast preparing to attack him he ran on towards an iceberg at some distance, kept running about always pursued by the bear; each time he rounded it he managed to hit a blow in the same spot on the iceberg, and in this manner he had soon made a cave, into which he hastened to creep, while the animal still hurried and followed the scent of his footmarks. Whenever the bear passed him he thrust at it with his tok (tool for making holes in the ice); each time he thus hit it some of the ice-cover dropped down from its back, and at length some bleeding was visible — snorting and roaring, it circled round the iceberg, but at length stopped short and fell down motionless. Iliarsorkik descended and found it to be dead; he cut out a piece of the flesh and made the best of his way home. Having arrived safely, he gave notice at the dwelling-places in the neighbourhood that whoever chose might go and fetch away some of the bear's flesh, and went along with his house-fellows, who had in the meantime fully recovered, to flense and cut it up on the following day. Having gone on for some time he saw a black spot on the ice which soon appeared to be the body of a dead man; further on they came across another one, and so on all the way — the corpses of people who had been on the point of starvation and had expired in making their attempt to reach the bear; a few of them had succeeded in reaching it and getting a bite of the flesh, but afterwards dropped on their way home, worn out with hunger and fatigue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Brothers Who Were Lost on Their Journey Up the Fiord

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; from two copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 48 'The Brothers who were lost on their Journey up the Fiord', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: One by one the kayakers who went up the fiord disappeared; the elder of the two brothers left is drawn by two old sorcerers to a shore of their many sons, his kayak smashed, a dish of berries offered with a human hand sticking up among them. Unable to be beaten at hook-and-crook, he is kept alive; his brother follows, gets his own kayak snatched to safety by the feigning brother, and at midnight escapes while the brother delays the pursuit by breaking every oar. Revenge comes in winter — the elder brother betrays the hiding cave, arrows kill all but one, and the last, escaping as a bird, is shot by an orphan boy's arrow and cut to pieces, his entrails sunk in the ocean's depths and left where the sun never shone.
summary.zh: 凡上峽灣的皮艇客一個接一個消失。留下的兄弟中，兄長先去尋人——被兩個老巫引上岸，皮艇被砸碎，一盆漿果中竟插著半只人手。他摔跤無人能敵，才保住性命；弟弟循跡而至，假裝不相識的兄長把他的皮艇搶到高處藏好，半夜放他逃走，又在追擊中逐一折斷船槳。冬日大軍復仇——兄長出賣藏身的巖洞，箭雨之中僅餘一人化鳥飛出，卻被練弓的孤兒一箭射中，屍遭肢解，腸臟一半沉入海底，一半留在太陽照不到的地方。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note records two variants: the old bachelor suffocated by the women's caresses; the sorcerer who flew at visitors like a bird striking off their heads, killed by a trained boy's arrow. Massacre and mutilation recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Several men were living together in the mouth of a fiord; each of them used to go out kayaking by himself, but it so happened that all those who went up the fiord entirely disappeared one after another. Two brothers, both strong and able men, were still left, and of these the eldest first went out in search of the lost ones. He kept close along shore; but having arrived at a certain spot, he could not master the strong tide, but was carried along by it to a place where two old people were standing, who by magic drew him to their shore. When he got upon land he saw numbers of people, who were all sons of the old couple; they seized his kayak, smashed it asunder, and put the pieces of it on the top of the turned-up boat. He was then asked to enter the house, and a dish of berries was put before him — but perceiving part of a human hand sticking up among them, he left it untouched. The people he had thus encountered were the murderers of his lost friends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 48 'The Brothers who were lost on their Journey up the Fiord'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At nightfall they entered to attack him also, and with this view they as usual took out a sealskin and spread it on the floor for a trying-match at hook and crook; seeing, however, that nobody was able to conquer him in this way, they dared not downright kill him. His kayak being destroyed, he was deprived of all means of returning. His brother in vain awaited his arrival, and therefore at length resolved to follow him; he took the very same course, and had the same fate, being likewise drawn towards the shore by the two old people — but before the young men could seize hold of his kayak, his own brother, who all the while had feigned to know nought of him, caught it up and placed it in safety on the top of the boat. At night he said to the men of the place that they might as well go to sleep, and that he would take charge of the stranger; but at midnight he suffered him to escape, and not till he believed he had gained a safe distance did he awake the people of the house and make known to them what had happened. The boat was quickly got down and put out in pursuit; the brother, who was given charge of the steering-oar, feigned to be pulling exceedingly hard, and in so doing purposely broke every oar he got in hand in order to delay the pursuit. Meanwhile the fugitive escaped them, and on reaching home went off in search of helpmates to the north as well as to the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 48 'The Brothers who were lost on their Journey up the Fiord'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the ensuing winter they started in great numbers to take revenge on the fiord people. When the latter had been apprised of their approach, the elder brother, who was still staying with them, said he would rescue them, and they had better go and hide themselves in a cave close by — but no sooner had the assailants arrived than the brother hastened to point out their hiding-place, and they commenced the attack, pouring their arrows into the cave, killing all but one, for whom there was not an arrow left. Presently, however, a bird came flying out of the cave; one of them quickly got an arrow from an orphan boy, who had just been practising bow-shooting, and hit the bird with it — and when they came to look more closely at it, the bird turned out to have been one of the men. They cut him to pieces, and at once took out his entrails; part of them were sunk in the depths of the ocean, and the rest brought to a place on which the sun never shone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 48 'The Brothers who were lost on their Journey up the Fiord'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Solitary Kayaker: Grief, Blood, and the White Whale

region.en: Northern three-windowed house and the solitary hunting-ground
region.zh: 北方的三窗大屋與獨享獵場

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 49 'The Solitary Kayaker', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A talkative rival pre-empts the solitary kayaker's private hunting-ground day after day — until the rival falls silent: his wife is dying. Going to console the widower, the visitor is seized by the throat, flung into the doorway, and has his spine broken against the door-posts; a widow's son whets his knife and cuts the murderer's back open, and a terrible slaughter ensues. The survivors ration dried capelins until the son drags home an immense white whale — the blood-filled boots chill the stepdaughter, who breaks in twain dead at the entrance, and is restored to life by the son's secret angakok spell.
summary.zh: 一名健談的對手日日搶佔獨釣客的私人獵場——直到對方一言不發：他的妻子快死了。登門慰問的訪客被扼喉、擲入甬道，脊背撞上門柱而死；寡婦之子磨利尖刀，從背後將那喪妻者剖開，血濺滿屋，一場屠殺隨之而起。倖存者靠定量分食乾魚度日，直到兒子拖回一頭巨大的白鯨——魚血灌靴的繼女雙腳冰冷、看山成雙，彎身入門時斷成兩截倒斃；兒子於燈滅之夜施咒，將她救活。此後三人安居，他娶了義妹。

sensitivity.note: Mourning-violence and sudden slaughter recorded as told in the 1875 source. The angakok son's secret identity is the tale's turn.

passages.text: There was once a kayaker who had only one certain hunting-place to which he always resorted, and whither he was never accompanied by any one else; he was well skilled in his craft, and generally brought home a great quantity of seals. Not far off, to the north of his habitation, lived a number of other people in a large house with three windows. One day he had started as usual for his solitary hunting-ground, but for the first time found it preoccupied by another hunter — on coming closer he recognised in him one of his northern neighbours. This man spoke to him and was so talkative that the other found it rather difficult to mind his work; at home he reported, 'To-morrow I intend to be off earlier and try to forestall him' — but on reaching the place the other man had already arrived, and was even more loquacious than on the first day; it was almost daybreak before they had begun their work. Trying again, starting while it was still pitch-dark, the other was on the spot, rowing close up to him — but to-day he did not speak at all; not until daybreak did he utter a single word, and then went away. The next day it was the same thing over again, he never spoke till sunrise: 'To-day she remained in bed altogether; the day before yesterday she fell sick, and all the while she is growing worse and worse' — speaking of his wife, and this was the reason why he had thus changed. 'If thou dost not meet me here to-morrow, thou mayst judge that she is still worse, and then pray look in upon us to-morrow and see how we are doing.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 49 'The Solitary Kayaker'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He did not meet his new comrade the next day, and therefore called on him the day after; entering the house he found all the men within, not one of them out kayaking that day. He entered the room and there remarked a man sitting far back upon the ledge and staring straight before him, and soon recognised him to be his former companion: his wife had died and he had already buried her. Observing the general silence, he rose and moved alongside the widower, saying, 'I have come to give thee some solace; thou wilt be sure to stand in need of some one to talk to thee at such an unhappy time: and if thou wouldst like it, I will bethink me of something to tell thee' — but at this the widower uttered some unintelligible words, at the same time looking very fierce and angry, suddenly advanced, took hold of the visitor by the throat, and threw him down into the doorway. Taking it all for a jest, he quickly got up and re-entered the room; but he was again seized and thrust right against the door-posts and broke his spine, which immediately caused his death. The murderer again with downcast eyes seated himself on the ledge; meanwhile a youth, the son of a widow, coolly proceeded to whet his knife, and when he had got it well sharpened, sprang up behind the widower and made a long cut on each side of his back; the blood rushed out, and in a few minutes he fell down dead. At this sight they all got infuriated and took to their knives, and a terrible slaughter ensued; the widow and her son, with an adopted daughter, were the only ones that remained unhurt, and having made their escape through the window, went to take up their abode in the storehouse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 49 'The Solitary Kayaker'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But subsequently the winter became very severe, and the frost fearfully keen, so that the widow's son at last had to give up hunting and remain indoors. They had almost finished their stock of provisions, only a few angmagsat (small dried fish) and a small bag with blubber still left, and accordingly could not afford to eat their fill every day; not till supper-time did the widow venture to share out their portions — the son then got two and a half fish, while she herself and her stepdaughter had one and a half. Owing to this sensible management they kept alive, though badly enough, because they always got a morsel of blubber besides. For three succeeding days they went on like this, but on the fourth the young man disappeared — he had only gone out to take a look round from some of the neighbouring heights. In the evening he put his weapons and tools to rights, and on the very next day returned home dragging an immense white whale with him; the women were transported with joy, and at once began to flense and cut it up — but presently the daughter complained of her feet being so dreadfully cold: the blood of the fish had got into her boots and filled them. Her mother pretended not to heed her, and told her to go on helping her; a little afterwards the girl said that she saw all the mountains double, and then she was ordered to go inside — the moment she bent down to descend through the entrance she broke in twain, and was dead on the spot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 49 'The Solitary Kayaker'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the evening the son wrought a spell upon the body of the deceased, and not till then was her mother aware of his being an angakok; they extinguished the lamps and he called forth the spirits, and restored her to life and health. They all remained living together at this place, and he afterwards married his adopted sister; at length they died there without removing to any other place, and without any accidents ever happening to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 49 'The Solitary Kayaker'; not verbatim.

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The wife's watchful hope, the stolen seal with its walrus-tooth towing-line, the stone rolled into the sea for a phantom walrus, the kayak hammered and stuffed with ice for a phantom iceberg calving, the fatted boasts to a starving father-in-law boiling dog's flesh, the raven-trap 'Two! — alas! one made its escape,' the dead daughter's name 'Nepisanguak' — until the last lie, a floating bit of whale-skin as a whale-carcass, leads the whole boat-fleet ness after ness to nothing, and they stop all his fibs by killing him then and there.
summary.zh: 妻癡望於門，他竊取同伴的海豹、炫耀海象牙拖繩；把石頭滾入海中冒充中叉的海象；把皮艇砸爛、懷揣冰塊，謊稱冰山崩塌壓頂；到斷糧煮狗肉的岳父家誇耀『倉庫都塞滿了』；以『抓到兩只——唉，跑了一只』的渡鴉陷阱哄騙；冒用亡女之名『尼皮桑瓜克』騙取珠串炊鍋。最後他拾起一片漂浮的鯨皮謊稱鯨屍，引得全隊大舟一岬又一岬地空尋——眾人厭極，就地將他殺死，斷了他所有的謊。

sensitivity.note: Same liar-type as Rasmussen's Qasiagssaq (cross-ref inuit-qasiagssaq-great-liar) but a different telling with distinct episodes. Killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Kasiagsak, who was living with a great many skilful seal-hunters, always returned in the evening without a catch of his own; when he was out, his wife, named Kitlagsuak, was always restless and fidgety, running out and in looking out for him, in the hope that he might be bringing home something — but he generally returned empty-handed. One day, being out in his kayak, he observed a black spot on a piece of ice, and it soon turned to be a little seal; his first intention was to harpoon it, but he changed his mind: 'Poor little thing! it is almost a pity. Perhaps it has already been wounded by somebody else; perhaps it will slide down in the water when I approach it, and then I need only take hold of it with my hands.' So saying he gave a shout, at which the seal was not slow to get down; presently it appeared close before the point of his kayak, but he called out still louder than before, and the seal went on diving up and down quite close to him. At length he made up his mind to chase and harpoon it; but somehow it always rose at a greater distance, and was soon entirely lost to him. 'Ye silly thing! ye are not easy to get at; but just wait till next time.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Another day he went seaward in bright fine weather; looking towards land he got sight of the other kayakers, and observed that one of them had just harpooned a seal, the others all hurrying on to his assistance. As to himself he never stirred, but remained quite unconcerned in his former place; he also noticed that the one who had caught the seal tugged it to the shore and made it fast to a rock on the beach, intending to return in pursuit of others. He instantly put further out to sea; when he had got quite out of sight he returned to the beach by a roundabout way, made straight for the other man's seal, and carried it off — the towing-line all around ornamented with walrus-teeth, and he greatly delighted at the prospect of getting home with this prize. His wife, wandering about in expectation, cried out at last, 'There is a kayak!' — shading her eyes with her hand, 'It looks like Kasiagsak, and he moves his arms like one tugging something along with him. Well, I suppose it will now be my turn to give you a share, and ye shall all get a nice piece of blubber.' As soon as he landed she hastened to ask, 'Where didst thou get that beautiful tugging-line?' 'This morning at setting out I thought it might come in handy, as I was bent on having a catch, and so I brought it out with me; I have kept it in store this long time.' She began the flensing and carving business, putting the head, the back, and the skin aside, all the rest as well as the blubber to make a grand feast upon; the other kayakers successively returned, and she took care to inform each separately that a seal was already brought home. But while they were sitting down to supper in the evening a boy entered: 'I have been sent to ask for the towing-line; as to the seal, that is no matter.' 'Didst thou tell me an untruth?' — 'To be sure I did' — 'What a shame it is that Kasiagsak behaves thus!' — he only made a wry face, 'Bah!' which made her quite frightened; and when they lay down to rest he went on pinching her and whistling until they both fell asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Another day, rowing about in his kayak, he observed a black spot away on a flake of ice; on nearing it he made it out to be only a stone. He glanced round towards the other kayakers, then suddenly feigned to be rowing hard up to a seal, lifting the harpoon ready to lance it — but presently went to hide behind a projecting point of the ice, from which he managed to climb it and roll the stone into the sea with a splash, making it all froth and foam; getting into his kayak again he made a great roar to call the others to his assistance. When they came up to him they observed he had no bladder — 'A walrus has just gone down with my bladder; do help me to catch sight of him; meantime I will turn back and tell that I have lanced a walrus.' He hurried landwards; his wife again shouted, 'A kayaker!' — 'I almost do believe it is Kasiagsak; do ye hear him in there?' Meantime he had approached the shore: 'In chasing a walrus I lost my bladder; I only came home to tell you this.' His wife came running into the house, in such a hurry she broke the handle of her knife — however, she did not mind: 'Now I can get a handle of walrus-tooth for my knife, and a new hook for my kettle.' In the evening Kasiagsak had chosen a seat on the hindermost part of the ledge, so that only his heels were to be seen; the other kayakers stayed out rather long, but the last of them on entering brought a harpoon-line and a bladder along with him: 'I think it is thine; it must have been tied round some stone and have slipped off; here it is.' 'Hast thou been telling us new lies?' — 'Why, yes; I wanted to play you a trick, you see.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Another day, kayaking along the coast, he remarked some loose pieces of ice away on a sandy beach at some distance; rowing up he went ashore, two women gathering berries watching his doings all along. They saw him fill his kayak with bits of broken ice, then wade down into the water till it reached his very neck, turn back and get upon the beach, set to hammering his kayak all over with stones, and having finally stuffed his coat with ice, turn towards home. At some distance he commenced shrieking aloud and crying, 'Ah me! a big iceberg went calving right across my kayak, and came down on the top of me' — his wife repeated his ejaculations, adding, 'I must go and see about some dry clothes for him'; large bits of ice came tumbling out of his clothes while he went on lamenting as if with pain — 'I had a very narrow escape' — his wife repeating the tale of his misfortunes to every kayaker on his return home. At last the two women who had seen him returned, and at once exclaimed, 'Is not that he whom we saw down below the sand-cliffs, stuffing his clothes with ice' — 'Dear me! has Kasiagsak again been lying to us?' Subsequently Kasiagsak went to pay a visit to his father-in-law: 'Why, what's the matter with you that your lamps are not burning, and ye are boiling dog's flesh?' — 'Alas!' answered the master, pointing to his little son, 'he was hungry, poor fellow! and having nothing else to eat we killed the dog.' Kasiagsak boastingly answered, 'Yesterday we had a hard job at home. One of the women and I had our hands full with the great heaps of seals and walruses that have been caught. I have got both my storehouses choke-full with them; my arms are quite sore with the work.' 'Who would ever have thought that the poor little orphan boy Kasiagsak should turn out such a rich man!' — and so saying he began crying with emotion; Kasiagsak feigned crying likewise. On parting the following day he proposed that his little brother-in-law should accompany him to bring back some victuals, adding, 'I will see thee home again'; on reaching home Kasiagsak busied himself in making a trap, taking scraps of frizzled blubber from his wife's lamp to thrust out as baits for the ravens — suddenly he gave a pull at the string, crying out, 'Two! — alas! one made its escape' — and then ran out and brought back a raven, which his wife skinned and boiled; his brother-in-law had to look to the other people for some food, and at his departure likewise received all his presents from them, and not from Kasiagsak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Another day he set off in his kayak to visit some people at a neighbouring station; having entered one of the houses he soon noticed that some of the inmates were mourning the loss of some one deceased. He questioned the others, and on hearing they had lost a little daughter named Nepisanguak, hastened in a loud voice to state, 'We have just got a little daughter at home, whom we have called Nepisanguak' — the mourning parents and relations exclaimed, 'Thanks be to thee that ye have called her by that name,' and wept, Kasiagsak also making believe to be weeping, but peeping through his fingers all the while. Later in the day they treated him richly; he went on, 'Our little daughter cannot speak plainly as yet; she only cries apangaja!' — the others said, 'She surely means scipangaja (sapangat, beads); we will give thee some for her' — at his departure he was loaded with gifts, such as beads, a plate, and some seal-paws; one of the men cried out to him, 'I would fain buy a kayak, and I can pay it back with a good pot; make it known to the people in thy place' — 'Give it to me; I have got a new kayak, but it is a little too narrow for my size.' At length he started along with his presents, the pot stuck upon the front part of his kayak; at home he said, 'Such a dreadful accident! a boat must surely have been lost; all these things I bring you here, I have found tossed about on the ice' — his wife hastened into the house to give her cracked old pot a smash, threw away the shoulder-blades that till now had served her instead of plates, ornamented her coat with beads, and proudly walked to and fro to make the pearls rattle. The next day a great many kayakers were announced; Kasiagsak instantly kept as far back on the ledge as possible. As soon as the kayakers put in to shore they called out, 'Tell Kasiagsak to come down and fetch off some victuals we have brought for their little daughter' — 'Why, they have got no daughter at all.' 'Go and ask Kasiagsak for the new kayak I bought of him' — 'He certainly has no new kayak.' At this information they quickly got up to the house, entered, taking their several gifts back, and last of all cutting the flaps ornamented with beads away from the wife's jacket; when the strangers were gone she said as before, 'Kasiagsak has indeed been telling a lie again.' His last invention: one day he found a small bit of whale-skin floating on the top of the water, and bringing it home said, 'I have found the carcass of a whale; follow me and I will show you it' — the boat was got out and they started; after a good while they asked him, 'Whereabout is it?' — 'Away yonder' — a little bit further, 'We shall soon get at it' — but when they had gone a long way from home without seeing anything like a floating whale, they got tired of Kasiagsak, and put a stop to all his fibs by killing him then and there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Revived Youth and the Under-World People
title.zh: 復活的少年與地下之民

region.en: Rock-cliff of the ingnersuit and the cliff-top house
region.zh: 地下之民的巖崖與崖頂之屋

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 51 'The Revived who came to the Under-world People', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Left before the five mourning days were over, the dead son is dug up by starving old housemates and chanted back to life — running headlong at the man, the woman, and himself until they all lie fallen. His father returns, disbelieves, kills him by touching him, and the old people revive him a second time; 'No, no! ye left me before the five mourning days were over, and therefore I will remain with those who have revived me.' Married to an ingnersuak-woman, he leads his foster-parents to the cliff that opens — 'do not look back' — but at the sight of the beautiful country with heaps of flesh and matak they turn for joy, the prow smashes on the rock, and they are left apart for ever, fed daily by the ingnersuit from their cliff-top house.
summary.zh: 喪期未滿五日便被拋下的死者，被斷糧的老夫婦掘出、唱咒復生——他橫衝直撞，把漢子、婦人、連自己都撞倒在地。生父不信，伸手一碰，他又倒斃；老夫婦再度唱咒救活。『不！你們喪期未滿就丟下我，我要留在救活我的人身邊。』娶了地下女子後，他引養父母去那會開合的巖崖——『千萬別回頭』——然而一見崖內美景與成堆的肉與鯨皮，二人歡喜忘誡回頭相望，船頭撞上峭壁粉碎，從此永隔；老夫婦在崖頂築屋，日日由地下之民送飯。

sensitivity.note: Five-day mourning period and grave-revival chant documented as told. Orpheus-type backward-glance taboo parallels the Greek cluster.

passages.text: A husband and a wife, with an only son, were living together with an old married couple who had got no children at all. On a certain day, while together on the fishing-place, the former lost their son, and left the place before the five subsequent mourning days were over, leaving the old childless people behind. Not knowing anyway to get food without assistance, the man said to his wife, 'Let us go up to the tomb' — 'Thou being a woman, must open the grave' — 'Thou being the man, ought to do so.' However, she proceeded to take away the top-stone, after which the man set himself to open the grave. When they had got the corpse taken out and had done chanting over it, it began to move, and after a while it rose up, and began running straight against the man. The woman now said to her husband, 'Stand steady' — the very same moment he was overturned, in the next she was herself thrown over, and lastly the youth also fell down. The old man first rose, and going up to him said, 'Now, dear, come along and stay with us' — and the revived youth went home with them, got a kayak, and became their provider.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 51 'The Revived who came to the Under-world People'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Once his real father came back to see what had become of the old people, who he almost expected had starved for want of food. Coming round the point, and seeing blood upon the stones on the beach, he thought, 'They must have been to the grave and taken away the corpse' — but coming closer, he observed marks of seal-flensing besides, and therefore inquired, 'Whoever might have caught these for you?' They made answer, 'Thy own son, whom we have restored to life again' — but he at once prepared to kill them, because he doubted the truth of this assertion and believed they were mocking him. The old man now said, 'Just wait a little; and if he then does not come, it is time enough to kill us!' Before he had finished speaking the son appeared from behind the point; they both cried out, 'Don't touch him at once!' — but the father could not forbear so doing, and consequently he again fell down dead on the spot. The old people again sang some magic lay over him, and by this means restored him to life; once more he moved, rose up, and ran right up to his father, whom he threw down, and likewise his foster-mother, but then stopped. His father would fain have taken him home to his true mother, but the son answered him, 'No, no! ye left me before the five mourning days were over, and therefore I will remain with those who have revived me' — and the father started off by himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 51 'The Revived who came to the Under-world People'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the youth returned in his kayak, but in a strangely silent mood — 'Why doestn't thou speak, dear?' — to which the son answered that he had gone and taken an ingnersuak-woman for a wife. The old people were sorry that he should have to leave them, and asked him if they might not accompany him; one day, on meeting an ingnersuak, he inquired of him whether he could bring them with him — he answered that they might come, but at the same time told him to warn them not to look back when they approached the rock which enclosed the abode of the ingnersuit, lest the entrance should remain shut for them. He told them this, and impressed on them all the way to keep their eyes fixed on the point of his kayak; they then instantly loaded the boat and made ready to depart. When they had reached the cliff and were rowing up to it, it forthwith opened; and inside was seen a beautiful country, with many houses, and a beach covered with pebbles, and large heaps of flesh and matak. Perceiving this, the old people for joy forgot the warning and turned round, and instantly all disappeared: the prow of the boat knocked right against the steep rock, and was smashed in, so that they all were thrown down by the shock. The son said, 'Now we must remain apart for ever; but build your house on yonder cliff: they will no doubt provide you with food.' They built their house on the cliff, and every day they got their meals without trouble from the ingnersuit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 51 'The Revived who came to the Under-world People'; not verbatim.
